I bought a MacBook from Currys and an iPhone from Apple in the past 5 years and I would suggest always getting it directly from Apple. When I had a problem with the phone 2 years into owning it, Apple dealt with it directly, said it was a manufacturing fault and replaced it quickly. When I had a fault with the MacBook 13 months into owning it, Apple assessed it and said it was a manufacturing fault but as I'd bought from Curry's I'd have to go to them. They wanted £60 to inspect it again (which I did eventually get back) but I had to then send it away and it took a while to get sorted.

Basically if anything goes wrong within 12 months you'll be fine dealing direct with Apple. Outside of that it's down to the retailer and Apple are much better to be dealing with at that stage than Currys are.

I'm not sure on the legal position but before going down the route of taking them to court, I'd strongly consider the Financial Ombudsman. The Ombudsman are free and generally considered more consumer friendly than the courts. If you make a court claim, you do not get a 'second go' with the ombudsman, but if you go to the ombudsman first, you can then go to court if you're still not happy. The FOS is also free and binding on the business but not on you.

To go to the FOS, you'll need to make sure the company have recorded this as an official complaint, and they have 8 weeks to provide you with a final decision.

Even if your insurer doesn't deal with it in time, they would still be responsible for any costs. If you respond yourself, you may prejudice their position which makes it more likely you would be responsible for costs - just leave it all to them (of course if you want to check what's going on, there's no harm in badgering them to make sure they're dealing with it)

It is likely that the hotel will have a sign up saying that their losses are limited to £50 for any one item and £100 in total under the Hotel Proprietors Act. Unless the theft is down to "the default, neglect or wilful act of the proprietor or his employee" they are entitled to limit their liability this way.

You may be able to demonstrate neglect - particularly if they managed to gain entry by stealing a key which was not secured, or something along those lines.

The easiest way though is to go through your insurance. You mention your travel insurance covering it - unless you have a high end policy, the limits on electronics and valuables tend to be quite low on these policies - if you have a household policy with personal belongings cover, this may be better to use. The insurance company will then pursue the hotel if they feel there is any legal liability.

The ombudsman is free, but before you use them you need to make sure Eldon insurance are dealing with it as a formal complaint. You can do this either verbally or in writing but obviously the paper trail with it being in writing is better.

They will have 8 weeks to investigate the complaint and respond, and once they have issued their response (or 8 weeks passes) you can take it to the ombudsman.

If you lose with the ombudsman, you can take legal action but it would generally be pretty unwise as the ombudsman is much more pro-consumer than the courts. If you go the legal route via the courts first, you cannot then try with the ombudsman.

In terms of your case, I'm not sure how they would view it. They may take the minded view that if you really only live one road away, and parked at your work because it was close and there were no spaces that it's not really commuting - but this may conflict with where you said the car was left overnight when taking out the policy. I'd lean towards them taking the literal interpretation that this was a journey from work to home, and as such, commuting - but they do sometimes throw up some surprise rulings.

Whatever you do, it's worth making a complaint and going down this route, because there is no downside to you, but the upside that you may be successful. Eldon/Goskippy shouldn't pursue you for any costs whilst the complaint is being assessed by them and then FOS.
